title: Tu or Lei?
body: Italian has two ways to say "you". Use "tu" with friends, family and children. Use "Lei" with strangers and in shops. With Lei, the verb takes the "he/she" form: parla, può.

title: Sono, sei, è
body: The verb "essere" (to be) changes with the person: io sono, tu sei, lui è, lei è. Italians often leave out io, tu and lui: "Sono uno studente" means I am a student.

title: Il, la and l'
body: Every noun is an "il" word or a "la" word. Most ending in -o take il: il numero. Most ending in -a take la: la mattina. Before a, e, i, o, u, both become l': l'ora. Some il words use lo: lo studente.

title: Hungry? Use avere
body: Italian says "I have hunger": ho fame, ho sete. Age works the same way: "Ho 25 anni" is "I have 25 years". Ho comes from the verb avere (to have). The h is silent.

title: Saying not: non
body: To say "not", just put non before the verb: capisco, non capisco. Nothing else changes. "Non c'è" means "there isn't".

title: Words that match
body: Describing words change their ending to match: alto for a man, alta for a woman, stanchi for a group. Words ending in -e, like felice, stay the same for men and women.

title: Verbs ending in -are
body: Many verbs end in -are, like parlare and lavorare. For "I", swap -are for -o: parlo, lavoro. For "you" (tu), use -i: parli. You can usually leave out io.
